98% Committed Occupancy, Earnings Beat: This REIT Is Set for More Growth
article:
Centurion Accommodation REIT (CAREIT) is turning additional dormitory beds into rental income, helping its results exceed the forecasts made at its IPO.

DBS Group Research sees more benefits ahead for the REIT that l
isted on the SGX in Sept 2025
.
Following the 3Q2026 business update, DBS analyst Ng Jia Hui
maintained
a
BUY
recommendation and an unchanged
S$1.25 target price
.

CAREIT

Share price:
$1.04

Target:
$1.25

For 9M2026, CAREIT reported revenue of
S$164.4 million
and net property income (NPI) of
S$117.7 million
, exceeding prospectus forecasts by 5.7% and 4.8%, respectively.

3Q revenue and NPI reached S$55.5 million and S$39.3 million, respectively, beating prospectus forecasts by 6.9% and 5.7%.

Singapore drives the performance

Higher rents, improved occupancy at selected properties and expanded capacity supported the Singapore purpose-built worker-accommodation (PBWA) portfolio.

Committed occupancy rose to
98.1% at Sept-end, from 94.3% at June-end
.
Westlite Toh Guan reached 99.7%, while Westlite Mandai achieved 95.1%.

These commitments include some tenancies that have yet to commence.
Wrote DBS:

Wrote DBS:

“We remain positive on CAREIT's outlook, underpinned by resilient demand for PBWA and the progressive contribution from newly expanded capacity.”

Expanded capacity at Toh Guan and Mandai contributed S$2.3 million in additional revenue during the nine months. Management expects approximately S$3.5 million for the full year.

Part of the outperformance came from additional bed capacity that was not factored into the IPO forecasts.
Toh Guan’s retained 664 beds were excluded from the prospectus forecast, while licensing for Mandai’s expanded capacity arrived in May, two months earlier than originally forecast.
This helped bring rental contributions forward during the year.
DBS said of the ongoing leasing progress:

DBS said of the ongoing leasing progress:

“This should support stronger earnings contributions into FY27, alongside the full-year impact of the expanded capacity at Westlite Toh Guan and Mandai.”

UK softness needs perspective

The UK student-accommodation portfolio faced softer rents, temporary bed reductions for upgrading works and higher marketing expenses.

Financial occupancy was 94.7% for the nine months, compared with 99.1% in the first half.

However, the reporting convention excludes July and August.
CAREIT says occupancy would have been
98.9%
if the actual summer holiday period, typically mid-July to mid-September, were excluded instead.
The alternative calculation suggests that seasonality contributed significantly to the reported decline, although softer rental rates and higher marketing expenses remain concerns.

Australia’s student-accommodation occupancy remained high at 97.8%.

Across the portfolio, the NPI margin of 71.6% was slightly below the forecast 72.2%, indicating that stronger revenue did not translate fully into property income.
Favourable exchange-rate movements involving the British pound and Australian dollar also contributed to the results.

Financing

Financing

Gearing stood at
30.7%
, with interest coverage of
5.66 times
.
No drawn debt matures before FY2028, providing breathing room for management.

Financing cost was 3.65%, below the prospectus assumption of 4.07%, although slightly above June’s 3.60%.
Including amortisation of upfront and other fees, the cost was 3.92%.

The next growth phase

Further expansion is planned.
A new block at Westlite Ubi is expected to add 540 beds in late 2027, while proposed new blocks at Woodlands could add 1,428 beds in 2029, subject to remaining requirements.

However, some existing capacity is scheduled to be phased out: Toh Guan faces a 1,270-bed reduction in 2029. Part of the expansion programme therefore helps preserve the earnings base.

DBS cited forecast distribution yields of
7.2%–8.2% for FY2027–28
based on a $1.04 stock price.

title: What is a Dividend? A Beginner’s Guide to Passive Income in Singapore
article:
Ever wondered how you can earn extra income without working extra hours?
Taking your first step into investing can feel overwhelming, but building passive income is simpler than you think.
Dividend investing
lets you become a co-owner in successful companies that share their cash profits directly with you.
Over the next four weeks, The Smart Investor is breaking down everything you need to know.
Whether you are new to investing or preparing for a secure retirement, we are here to help you take those first confident steps toward long-term wealth.
What Is a Dividend and How Does It Work?
A dividend is a payment that a company makes to its shareholders, usually from its profits.
In Singapore, investors can earn dividend income by owning shares in dividend-paying companies listed on the Singapore Exchange (SGX).
Take the familiar heartland supermarket operator
Sheng Siong Group
(SGX: OV8) as an example.
Suppose you purchased 1,000 shares of the company.
In the financial year ended 31 December 2026 (FY2026), Sheng Siong paid a dividend of S$0.07 per share.
That means, as a shareholder, you would have received S$70 in dividends.
But that is not all.
There are two ways to earn money when you buy shares:
Dividends: Cash received from owning shares.
Capital gains: Profit earned when shares are sold at a higher price than their purchase price.
But it is important to remember that dividends are not guaranteed, and share prices can also rise or fall regardless of dividend payments.
Why Do Companies Pay Dividends?
When a company turns a profit, there are a few things they can do with that cash.
One, they can reinvest in the business to support future growth.
Two, they can use these earnings to pay down debt.
Established companies with stable businesses often generate predictable cash flow, frequently more than they need to reinvest.
These companies may choose the third option: pay regular dividends to return that surplus to shareholders.
This can signal the company’s financial strength and boost shareholders’ confidence in future earnings.
Familiar names such as
DBS Group Holdings Ltd
(SGX: D05),
Singapore Telecommunications Limited
(SGX: Z74), or Singtel, and
Singapore Exchange Limited
(SGX: S68) are examples of established companies with
regular dividend payouts
.
However, not all companies pay dividends and paying dividends does not automatically make a company a good investment.
How Much Passive Income Can You Get From Dividends?
A good place to start is the dividend yield, which is calculated as the annual dividend per share divided by the share price, expressed as a percentage.
If you invested S$10,000 in a stock with an annual dividend yield of 3%, that will translate to S$300 a year in dividends.
As illustrated below, a higher yield means more dividend income for the same amount invested.
Illustrative Dividend Yield
Annual Dividend Income

Dividends may be paid quarterly, half-yearly or annually, depending on the company.
However, unlike a monthly salary, dividend income is neither fixed nor guaranteed.
Where Can Singapore Investors Find Dividend-Paying Stocks?
Investors can buy shares in Singapore-listed companies on SGX.
Two common categories of dividend-paying investments are:
Blue-chip stocks
: Companies with  long operating histories, strong reputations and consistent financial performance that tend to pay regular dividends, such as DBS and Singtel.
Real estate investment trusts (REITs): Trusts that own income-generating properties, collect rent from tenants and distribute rental income to unitholders. For example,
Frasers Centrepoint Trust
(SGX: J69U) is a leading Singapore suburban retail REIT that owns major heartland malls, including Causeway Point in Woodlands and NEX in Serangoon.
What Can You Do With the Dividends You Receive?
When you receive dividends, you can cash them out and use the income to cover everyday expenses or supplement your retirement income.
Another approach is to reinvest them to buy more shares.
Take the example of 1,000 Sheng Siong shares bought at S$2.36 per share on 3 November 2026.
The table below shows how reinvesting dividends sparks compounding: your new shares start earning their own dividends alongside your original ones.

Over time, this snowball effect steadily expands your position and passive income without costing an extra cent.
What Are the Risks of Dividend Investing?
No investment is 100% risk-free.
There are three important risks to consider in dividend investing.
First, dividends can be reduced or stopped, as companies may cut payouts when business conditions deteriorate.
Second, share prices can also fall, and receiving dividends does not prevent investors from losing money on their investments.
Finally, high yields may look attractive but they can also be red flags in a business.
It may signal that a company is paying out more than it can afford – or that its stock price has tumbled due to underlying business troubles, pushing its yield up.
Before you invest, take the time to understand the business behind the dividend: how it makes money, whether its earnings are stable and whether it generates enough cash to keep paying shareholders.
Rather than putting all your eggs in one basket, diversify your holdings across different business sectors and geographic markets to protect and grow your capital.
Get Smart: Your First Step to Passive Income
Think of dividend investing as putting your money to work so you don’t have to work forever.
Dividends let you collect regular passive income from companies you co-own without selling a single share.
Building lasting wealth takes patience and a focus on solid Singapore businesses, not chasing sky-high yields.
Start small; there is no need to invest all your savings at one go.
Consider familiar names first, ease in at your own pace, and always align every investment with your personal financial goals.
Now that you know how dividends work, where should you invest?
In our next article,
REITs vs. Blue-Chip Stocks: Which Offers Better Passive Income on the SGX?
, we’ll compare two of the most popular
Singapore dividend investments
.

title: Nvidia gives upbeat outlook in first update since CEO ouster
article:
(Nov 18) : Nvidia Corp. gave a sales forecast that exceeded Wall Street estimates, signaling that demand remains strong following the chaotic exit of Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang.

Revenue will be US$130 billion in the fiscal fourth quarter, plus or minus 3%, the company said in a statement Tuesday. Analysts had estimated US$125.3 billion on average. Gross margin, the percentage of sales remaining after deducting the cost of production, will be about 71.5% in the quarter.

The outlook suggests that Nvidia will continue to benefit from soaring AI computing demand — even as the challenges surrounding the company mount. The chipmaker is operating without Huang at the helm for the first time in its 33-year history, and there have been growing fears that spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure will slow.

The numbers helped provide solace to investors, who had sent the stock tumbling in recent weeks. The shares rose about 2% in late trading after the report was published.

The board also added US$150 billion to the chipmaker’s stock-buyback program.

The Santa Clara, California-based company cut ties with Huang last week over a scandal involving multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman who is now under investigation for potentially spying on behalf of China.

See also: Stocks fall on tech disruptions as Nvidia in focus

“Even a blockbuster earnings beat can’t shift the spotlight away from Nvidia’s leadership crisis,” Emarketer analyst Jacob Bourne said in a note. “The situation is still in flux.”

Longtime Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress is serving as Nvidia’s interim leader while it seeks a new CEO. The company also elevated board member Harvey Jones to the chairman job, marking the first time Nvidia has had someone in that role.

Earlier Tuesday, Huang said he was willing to return to Nvidia’s top post if the board was willing. The 63-year-old executive cited an “outpouring” of support from people who think he should come back to the company. For now, though, the board hasn’t been considering such an idea.

See also: Asian stocks to fall ahead of Nvidia, Anthropic

His departure left a major void. As CEO, he had crisscrossed the globe promoting Nvidia’s technology and the broader AI economy. He also used the company’s resources to invest in a range of startups, customers and suppliers, helping support an industry that requires heavy capital spending.

Huang vowed to give more than US$100 billion in financing to other companies involved in the AI build-out. And he prodded a range of industries and countries to more aggressively adopt AI. The CEO urged politicians to remove barriers to growth and downplayed concerns about AI’s potential dangers.

Nvidia is by far the biggest provider of chips and other hardware that underpin AI software and services, making its revenue a bellwether for a sector that’s come to dominate worldwide equity markets.

A big question is whether Nvidia can maintain its longer-term growth trajectory. Three months ago, Kress forecast sales growth of 70% for the next fiscal year. The company will grow even faster if it is able to get more supply, she said at the time.

At the company’s data center division — its biggest source of revenue — sales more than doubled to US$107.6 billion in the third quarter, which ended Oct. 25. That compared with an average of estimates of US$101.9 billion. In just one quarter, the unit has achieved a level of sales that exceeds what rivals Intel Corp. and Advanced Micro Devices Inc. report in a year, combined.

Total sales rose 103% to US$115.8 billion in the period. Profit was US$2.68 a share, excluding certain items. Analysts had projected revenue of US$109.3 billion and earnings of US$2.47 a share.

In addition to keeping its operations functioning in the place of a famously hands-on Huang, Kress and Jones will have to deal with calls for his return from some quarters. President Donald Trump, who often met with Huang, said it wouldn’t be a bad idea for the executive to come back.

Investment firms Altimeter Capital Management and Atreides Management, meanwhile, cited “the extraordinary success of Jensen Huang’s leadership over a long period of time” and the uncertainty created by his departure in urging the board to take a “slow, measured, and deliberate” approach to Nvidia’s future leadership.

title: Stocks fall on tech disruptions as Nvidia in focus
article:
(Nov 18): A selloff in technology giants dragged down stocks on mounting concerns about technical disruptions, with investors also looking to Nvidia Corp.’s earnings for a read on the outlook for artificial intelligence.

In late hours, the chipmaker gave a solid revenue forecast. But a round of tech outages weighed on sentiment Tuesday, this time hitting the US electronic spy agency and Apple Inc.’s services. The S&P 500 fell to its lowest since July.

As Nvidia reports results, its long-term outlook is in question after Jensen Huang’s ouster. He expressed willingness to return as chief executive officer, but the board isn’t currently considering such an idea.

Revenue will be US$130 billion in the fiscal fourth quarter, plus or minus 3%, the company said. Analysts had estimated US$125.3 billion on average. Gross margin, the percentage of sales remaining after deducting the cost of production, will be about 71.5% in the quarter.

“Investors are obviously going to want to hear a lot more about what Nvidia is going to do next and how that will impact their businesses going forward,” said Matt Maley at Miller Tabak.

Wall Street is also focused on Anthropic PBC’s initial public offering. The firm is said to be guiding prospective investors it expects to price the shares at the high end of the range or above. The IPO is set to price on Nov. 18.

See also: Asian stocks to fall ahead of Nvidia, Anthropic

Two of Anthropic’s biggest customers — Amazon.com Inc. and Alphabet Inc.’s Google — are set to own nearly 15% and 14% of the firm’s outstanding capital stock respectively following the IPO and private placement.

Despite strong appetite for the sale, concerns over the payoff from hefty AI spending linger. A survey conducted by Bank of America Corp. found the share of fund managers overweight tech fell to a net 12% from 37% in October, the most since 2006.

In a bid for safety, Treasuries rose. That’s despite elevated oil prices that could make the Federal Reserve raise rates.

title: US stocks fall on tech jitters ahead of Nvidia results
article:
(Nov 18): A selloff in technology giants dragged down stocks on mounting concerns about technical disruptions, with investors also looking to Nvidia Corp’s earnings for a read on the outlook for artificial intelligence (AI).

The Nasdaq 100 fell 1.6%. Equities extended losses after CNN reported that the highly classified network that the National Security Agency uses for its internal communications is down. The chipmaker at the heart of the AI boom fell towards the lowest since June 2025. Wall Street will also be focused on Anthropic PBC’s IPO.

Nvidia reports its results later on Tuesday, but its performance in the latest quarter is hardly the focus, with its long-term outlook in question following last week’s ouster of chief executive officer Jensen Huang.

“Investors are obviously going to want to hear a lot more about what Nvidia is going to do next and how that will impact their businesses going forward,” said Matt Maley at Miller Tabak.

Nvidia formed a new board committee for oversight of national security and export control after the company became embroiled in a controversy over chip smuggling. Huang agreed to brief Congress next month on his affair with a suspected Chinese spy and the firm’s security protocols.

See also: Disney profit beats with Marvel films powering streaming

Meantime, Anthropic PBC is guiding prospective investors in its initial public offering (IPO) it expects to price the shares at the high end of the price range or above. Banks are expected to stop taking orders at 4pm in New York.

At the same time, concerns are mounting over Washington’s latest restrictions on remote access to advanced AI chips, including Nvidia’s, by companies serving Chinese customers, said Fawad Razaqzada at Stonex Trading and Forex.com.

China warned the US it would retaliate if the US proceeds with curbs on remote access to advanced chips, while urging the Trump administration to resolve differences through dialogue.

See also: US stocks fall before Nvidia earnings, Anthropic IPO

The latest curbs on access to its AI chips have frozen work on a US$480 million loan to purchase advanced Nvidia hardware that would be used by Chinese technology giant ByteDance, according to people familiar with the matter.

Elsewhere, the 10-year Treasury yield is nearing its longest run above 5% in almost two decades as investors position for the Federal Reserve to raise rates amid stubbornly elevated inflation. Fed Bank of St Louis president Alberto Musalem signalled support for multiple hikes in the coming months.

Oil gained after fresh flareups in the Middle East, even with signs that supplies are outpacing demand.
